title: Sort 0s, 1s, 2s in one pass (Dutch National Flag: three pointers).
shortTitle: Sort 0s, 1s, and 2s in One Pass (Dutch National Flag)
keyPoints: Three pointers (low, mid, high) partition the array into zeros, ones, and twos in a single pass
When mid sees a zero, swap with low and advance both low and mid
When mid sees a one, just advance mid because ones belong in the middle
When mid sees a two, swap with high and decrement high but do NOT advance mid
The non-advance on the two-swap is the most common bug and the key interview detail
Time complexity is O(n) with O(1) extra space, beating general O(n log n) sorts for this special case
The same three-way partition is the core of three-way quicksort for arrays with many duplicates

s1_definition.oneliner: Low, mid, and high pointers partition the array into zeros, ones, and twos in a single pass with O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Dutch National Flag** – an algorithm that sorts an array containing only three distinct values (0, 1, 2) in a single linear pass.
- **Three pointers** – `low` marks the boundary of the zeros region, `high` marks the boundary of the twos region, and `mid` scans the unknown portion.
- **Invariant** – everything before `low` is a confirmed zero, everything between `low` and `mid` is a confirmed one, and everything after `high` is a confirmed two.
- **Swap rules** – a zero at `mid` swaps with `low` and advances both; a two at `mid` swaps with `high` and decrements only `high`; a one at `mid` just advances `mid`.
- **Asymmetry** – after a two-swap `mid` stays because the incoming value from `high` is unexamined; after a zero-swap `mid` advances because the incoming value from `low` is already processed.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India classifies each of the day's transactions on Rajesh's account into three risk buckets: low risk as zero, medium as one, and high as two. The bank wants them physically reordered so all low-risk come first, then medium, then high, in one sweep. Three clerks work the row: one pushes low-risk items to the left end, one pushes high-risk items to the right end, and one walks the middle sorting each item into place. In a single walk the row is grouped perfectly.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Dutch National Flag algorithm sorts an array of only three values in a single pass using three pointers. A low pointer marks where the next zero goes, a high pointer marks where the next two goes, and a mid pointer scans the unknown region. While mid is at or before high, you look at the value at mid: a zero swaps with low and advances both low and mid, a one just advances mid, and a two swaps with high and decrements high without advancing mid.

The subtle rule that makes it correct is the asymmetry on the two case. When you place a two by swapping with high, the value that comes back to mid has not been examined yet, so you must not advance mid. But when you place a zero by swapping with low, the value that comes to mid has already passed through the low region, so advancing mid is safe. Getting that wrong is the classic bug, and being able to explain exactly why is what separates a correct answer from a memorized one.

The algorithm runs each step either advancing mid or shrinking high, so the unknown region shrinks every iteration, giving linear time and constant space. Compared with the counting alternative, which also runs in O(n), the Dutch National Flag does a true single pass and moves actual objects rather than overwriting values, which matters when the elements are records rather than bare integers.

In the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to group a day's transactions by risk level (zero for low, one for medium, two for high) into a review queue so reviewers could clear low-risk items fast and focus on high-risk ones. The queue held real transaction objects, so the in-place swap approach preserved their identity while grouping them in a single pass over a large day.

Remember one sentence: three pointers, one pass, and never advance mid after swapping a two to the back.
